sentences.text: Which records a young software company can show an investor, what each one proves and where the proof stops
How to weigh the records of an early-stage software company: ownership, rights, share sales, tax filings, security and reported numbers, and their limits.

An early-stage software company hands an investor a folder, and the folder mixes documents of very different standing: registers the law requires, contracts a court would read, and slides written last week.
This brief sorts that material by the kind of claim each item can support.
Six records come up in turn: shareholdings, ownership of the code, the sale of shares, the tax elections of founders, product security practice and the open source components inside the product.
For each it reports what a public source says about the rule behind the record, and then separates that report from analysis of how a reader might test it.
One more section covers the figures a company reports on its own behalf, where public sources say least.
The brief closes with questions to put to a company, and with a plain account of what a review of documents cannot establish.
The brief describes how the subject works in general.
It is about no company and is not an assessment of any.
It is general information for investors.
It is not legal, tax or investment advice.

sentences.text: Eight checks an investor can run on a company whose product depends on a model, and what each one leaves unanswered
Eight checks for diligence on an early-stage company that depends on a model: data, supplier, security, evidence, claims, rules and ownership.
Investors who look at an early-stage software company are used to checking the entity, the cap table, the customers and the code.
A product that depends on a model adds questions those checks do not reach, and this brief is organized around them.
It sets out eight checks, running from the model's role and the data behind it to the supplier, security, proof of performance, public claims, regulation and ownership of outputs.
Each check names the public sources behind it, describes the documents a company might hold, and says what that evidence cannot establish.
The sources come from standards bodies, regulators, a security project and model suppliers' own documentation.
The brief reports what they say and keeps its analysis apart, marked as analysis.
It makes no assessment of any company, offers no recommendation to invest, and names no company.
It closes with questions to put to a company or to counsel.
This brief is general information for investors.
It is not legal, tax or investment advice.

sentences.text: How an organization and an early-stage founder can set out what each side expects in writing
For organizations working with early-stage founders: six kinds of arrangement, the ownership and data questions they raise, and what to put in writing.
Organizations that work with early-stage founders often agree on the spirit of an arrangement and leave the details unwritten.
This brief goes through the details that tend to be missed and explains why each deserves a line in a signed document.
It sorts common arrangements into six kinds: referral and resale, integration and listing, co-development, pilots, supplier terms and program participation.
It then follows the questions that cut across them.
Who owns what gets built?
How do copyright and patent rules treat work done by two parties?
What do open-source licenses ask of an organization that bundles a product?
What do data protection and security expectations look like in a contract?
When does the way people are directed make them employees rather than contractors?
What changes when a partner is paid in shares?
Each section reports what a public source says, drawn from statutes, agency pages and standards publications, and separates that report from analysis.
A table compares the structures, and a closing list gives questions that either side can bring to counsel.
The brief names no company and describes no particular arrangement.
It makes no promise of an introduction, a partnership or funding, and it does not recommend a structure.
It also lists what its sources cannot show, including state law, other countries and changes to rules after the evidence was read.
This brief is general information for partners.
It is not legal, tax or investment advice.

sentences.text: Four ways a company can host a new software product, and what each one settles about ownership, people and control
Four routes for a new software product inside a company, read through ownership, equity for staff, parent control and small-business rules.
Teams inside established companies often have a product idea that sits awkwardly beside the main business.
This brief looks at where such a product can live and treats the choice as a legal and organizational decision as much as a product one.
It compares four routes, running from a small team inside the parent to a separately owned company with outside shareholders, and a fourth in which the parent licenses its technology to someone else.
For each route it reports what public sources say about the mechanism and then separates that report from analysis.
The same questions run through every route.
Who holds title to the code the team writes?
Can staff who move hold shares?
What can the parent still decide?
Which public programs count a parent's ownership against a new venture?
What is at stake for the parent's own shareholders if shares are distributed to them?
What has to be separated in systems and data?
The brief ends with questions to put to counsel and with a plain statement of the limits of its sources, which are federal rules plus one state's company law.
No company is named, no particular arrangement is described and no corporate client is claimed.
This brief is general information for corporate teams.
It is not legal, tax or investment advice.
